notes.meaning: Isaiah receives a prophetic vision about the fall of the empire of Babylon. The word burden means a heavy, serious message of judgment from God. Although Babylon was not yet the dominant world power in Isaiah's day, God showed him its future rise and ultimate downfall to give comfort and hope to His people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many critical scholars question whether Isaiah wrote this chapter, arguing that its detailed description of Babylon's fall shows it was written much later during the Babylonian exile.

notes.meaning: God commands a signal flag to be raised high on a bare hilltop where everyone can see it. Shouts and waving hands summon the attacking armies to march straight into the grand gates of Babylon's rulers. God Himself is calling these forces together to carry out His purpose.

God speaks of the incoming conquerors as His sanctified warriors, meaning people He has specially set apart for a task, not that they are personally holy. He gave them power and courage to execute His righteous anger against Babylon. Even though these pagan soldiers seek their own glory, God uses their fierce pride to accomplish His triumph.

A loud rumble echoes across the mountains as armies from many nations gather for battle. Cyrus's army was made up of soldiers from various kingdoms, including the Medes and Persians. Behind all this military commotion, the Lord of hosts is the One organizing and directing the troops.

The invading armies march from distant lands at the far edge of the known world to bring ruin upon Babylon. The Lord Himself leads them, using these foreign soldiers as instruments of His righteous anger. Their mission is to sweep across the land and break its power completely.

Babylon is warned to weep and wail because the Day of the Lord is rushing toward them. In the Bible, the Day of the Lord is a time when God steps in to judge evil and set things right. This sudden ruin comes from the Almighty, leaving no way for the city to resist.

When judgment strikes, Babylon's defenders will lose all their strength and courage. Their hands will drop limply to their sides, unable to lift a weapon, and their brave hearts will melt away like wax. The shock of being attacked so suddenly will leave them completely helpless.

Sudden panic grips the people of Babylon, bringing agony like the sudden pains of a woman giving birth. They will stare at each other in frozen shock and disbelief as their city is overrun. Their faces will burn with fear and distress as all hope vanishes.

The Day of the Lord arrives with fierce, unsparing justice against a corrupt empire. It is called cruel not because God lacks goodness, but because His punishment falls with terrifying severity upon unrepentant sinners. The Lord will strip the land of its wealth and wipe out the wicked who lived there.

The prophet describes total darkness falling over the land, as if the sun, moon, and stars refuse to shine. In biblical poetry, this darkening of the skies depicts the sudden end of a nation's glory and the terror of God's judgment. All joy, guidance, and hope are cut off when the Lord turns out their light.

differ.view: These cosmic signs point to literal disturbances in the sun, moon, and stars that will accompany the final judgment at the end of the age.

notes.meaning: God announces that He will punish Babylon's vast empire for its cruelty and wicked deeds. Above all, He aims His judgment at their boastful pride and ruthless arrogance. Human tyrants may feel invincible, but the Lord can quickly bring down the proudest rulers.

The slaughter in Babylon will be so severe that surviving human beings will become extremely rare. Men will be harder to find than the finest gold imported from Ophir. The invading army will not accept bribes or gold to spare human lives.

God pictures the fury of His anger as an earthquake that shakes heaven and earth out of their places. This dramatic language shows how completely God will overthrow Babylon's kingdom and disrupt human security. Believers are reminded that only the Lord and His kingdom remain unshakable when worldly powers fall.

When the invader strikes, Babylon's foreign residents, traders, and hired troops will scatter in wild panic. Like a frightened gazelle fleeing hunters or sheep with no shepherd, everyone will run back to their own homelands. None of Babylon's allies will stay behind to help defend her.

Anyone caught inside the city will be struck down by the sword without mercy. Whether people try to hide in their homes or run through the streets, the conquerors will show no favor. The sentence against Babylon means complete military defeat and death for its defenders.

The invading soldiers will commit the horrific atrocities typical of ancient warfare, killing infants, looting houses, and assaulting wives. This terrible suffering was a bitter taste of the same cruelty Babylon had once inflicted on other nations, including Judah. God reveals the ugly reality of war to show how thoroughly worldly pride leads to ruin.

God specifically names the Medes as the power He will send against Babylon. This fierce nation from the north and east could not be bought off with gifts of silver or gold. They fought not for ransom, but to destroy Babylon's power completely.

The Medes and their allies were famous for their large bows and deadly archery. In their fury, they would spare neither strong young warriors nor defenseless little children. Their cold lack of pity shows the terrifying completeness of the judgment God permitted to fall upon Babylon.

Babylon was celebrated across the ancient world as the jewel of empires, renowned for its dazzling beauty and power. Yet God determined that it would end in total overthrow, just as Sodom and Gomorrah were wiped out long before. Its architectural splendor could not save it from divine justice.

differ.view: Because ancient Babylon declined gradually rather than being destroyed in an instant like Sodom, the city must be rebuilt in the future to face a sudden, cataclysmic destruction.

notes.meaning: Once brought down, Babylon would never again become a thriving city or a home for people. Even wandering desert nomads would refuse to pitch their tents on its ruins, and shepherds would not bring their sheep to graze there. Over the centuries, the once-bustling capital truly turned into an abandoned wasteland.

Instead of human citizens, wild desert animals and eerie nighttime creatures will roam the ruins. Ostriches will nest among the collapsed walls, and wild goats will leap across the rubble. The places where royalty once walked will belong entirely to wild beasts.

Howling hyenas and jackals will make their dens in the abandoned fortresses and luxury palaces of Babylon. God had already set the timetable for this empire's downfall, and its days of worldly glory were numbered. The ruin of this proud empire reminds God's people that earthly kingdoms pass away, but the Lord's word always stands.
